article_text:
Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace have begun their international press tour to promote their movie, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping .

The duo kicked things off in Sydney, the home country of Zada, who plays young Haymitch Abernathy.

Grace will play tribute Maysilee Donner in the film, set for U.S. release on November 20, 2026.

RELATED: Everything We Know About The ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Movie So Far

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is directed by Francis Lawrence from a screenplay by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie, based on the adaptation and novel by Suzanne Collins.

The film follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Zada) from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes.

Set in the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games , the story follows Haymitch into the arena, where he forms an unlikely alliance with fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Grace) and joins a coalition determined to challenge the Capitol’s control under President Snow (Ralph Fiennes).

As the competition unfolds, Haymitch risks everything to take down the Games from within the arena — setting in motion the rebellion that will change Panem forever.

The cast includes Joseph Zada, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Ben Wang. Other actors featured include Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, and Kelvin Harrison Jr.

article_text:
ザ・ノース・フェイス（THE NORTH FACE）の創業60周年を記念したアートエキシビション「EXPLORING WITH NATURE｜自然とともに探求すること」が、11月9日（月）まで、京都のTHE NORTH FACE STANDARD 京都で開催されている。

1966年の創業以来、自然への敬意と探求心をブランドの理念に掲げてきたザ・ノース・フェイス。本展では、自然と人間の関係をテーマに、異なる領域で活動する4名のアーティストの作品を紹介する。

参加するのは、アメリカを拠点に自然現象を取り入れた作品を制作するサム・フォールズ、1960年代末に登場した「もの派」の主要作家である菅木志雄、写真やフィールドレコーディングを通して人間と非人間、場所の記憶を探る濵本奏、そして日本の伝統技法「乾漆」を用いて生命や自然の神秘を表現する小梛真弓の4名。

石や木、金属と空間の関係を問い続ける菅の実践から、写真、音、漆といった多様なメディアを通じた表現まで、それぞれの作品は自然を単なる鑑賞対象ではなく、人間と関わり合う存在として捉えている。

本展が問いかけるのは、未知の場所へ踏み出すことだけではない「探求」のあり方だ。身近な自然の変化に目を向け、人間もまた自然の一部であることを再認識する。アウトドアブランドの理念と現代アートの実践が交差する展覧会となる。

Donald Insall, doyen of conservation architects, who has died aged 100, was very clear about the distinction between preserving buildings and conserving them. “Preservation,” he pronounced, “is what you do for marmalade.” Though Insall could see the value of preservation, he was an adroit conservationist rather than a stodgy marmalade maker, always seeing how historic buildings could be revived and put to new uses.

Marshalling teams of architects, craftsmen and builders, he brought Windsor Castle back from the brink following the devastating “ annus horribilis ” fire of 1992. The exacting rescue scheme encompassed a range of strategies, from complete restoration to renewal in spirit. “As well as keeping things as they were, or putting them back as one thinks they were – which is chancy and not the main aim – we had to find new solutions to parts that had been irreparably destroyed,” Insall told Country Life in 2018.

Other high-profile projects included the renovation of Kelmscott Manor, the Oxfordshire country home of the writer, designer and socialist William Morris, following its acquisition by the Society of Antiquaries in 1961, and the restoration of Kedleston Hall in Derbyshire, Robert Adam’s Palladian masterpiece, now in the care of the National Trust. “Kedleston was our first big job,” Insall recalled. “I used to take a scooter on the train, hop off at Derby and go to the hall, where I was met by the butler and the dogs. Once or twice, Lord Scarsdale, the owner, came on the back of the scooter for a ride around the estate.”

Insall was also involved in the lengthy rebuilding of Wotton House in Buckinghamshire, which had previously been remodelled by John Soane following a fire in 1820. Derelict and teetering on the brink of destruction, it was bought in 1957 by the enterprising Elaine Brunner, daughter of King George V’s valet, who had first arrived there, chauffeured by an antique dealer friend, to scavenge columns to adorn her swimming pool and then embarked on a decades-long programme of restoration.

Commissioned by custodians of the country’s most significant historic buildings, from town halls to royal palaces, Insall changed the scope and ambition of conservation practice, shaping pioneering approaches to heritage management at a time when historic buildings were widely seen as impediments to progress rather than assets to be cherished. In deftly addressing issues of heritage, sustainability and contemporary use, his approach has a renewed resonance and relevance. When Insall once worked for the College of Arms, he was granted a personal coat of arms. Aptly, he chose the motto “Bring Forth the Best”.

The son of Phyllis (nee Hill) and William Insall, he was born in Bristol into a family of long established manufacturers of traditional luggage, such as trunks, cricket bags and portmanteaux. He attended Bristol grammar school, and his interest in architecture was piqued when his father commissioned and built a new family home at Henleaze, in the north of the city. During the blitz, Insall witnessed the wartime destruction of Bristol’s ancient churches and historic buildings, and in 1942 started architectural studies at the Royal West of England Academy School of Architecture . He saw wartime service from 1944 in the Coldstream Guards, completing his education after being demobbed in 1948.

Insall studied civic design in London at the Royal Academy Schools and later at the RA’s School of Planning. In 1951 he was a Lethaby scholar with the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, the organisation founded by William Morris in 1877 in response to the activities of Victorian architects, whose misconceived enthusiasm for restoration often caused calamitous damage. As a Lethaby scholar, Insall worked with and learned from an array of traditional craftsmen, including thatchers and lime plasterers, going on to spend 18 months measuring and surveying Winchester college for the medieval historian John Harvey .

It proved a formative education in which he got to know and understand historic buildings from different periods. He claimed to have no favourites. “I love them all,” he said, relishing how social change was reflected in architecture. “It’s all part of a lively continuity.” What also mattered to him was not just the quality of individual buildings, but their wider contextual relationships with streets, towns and cities. The role of conservation architects was, Insall believed, to help make “every place to be truly more itself”.

Insall initially joined Phillimore and Jenkins, a London-based practice specialising in the restoration of country houses in the greatly altered postwar milieu. In 1958, together with a fellow Lethaby scholar, Peter Locke, he founded Donald Insall Associates, working from the kitchen table in his flat in Belgravia. His father and then his wife, Libby (nee Moss), a lawyer, whom he married in 1964, did the accounts. From these tentative beginnings, the practice is now over 100 strong, operating out of eight offices across England and Wales.

With modernism then in the ascendancy, it was a bleak time for historic buildings. Country houses that did not find a saviour were all too often demolished, as were urban swathes of Victorian and Georgian terraces. While conservation fired Insall’s imagination, taking an interest in old houses was regarded as perplexingly antiquarian, as he recounted to Country Life. “Nice to meet you, but when will your father be coming?” asked the builder on one early job.

Insall’s 1968 study of Chester was a landmark for urban conservation and town planning. Undertaken as a part of a government pilot project surveying four historic towns (the others were Bath, Chichester and York), it recognised for the first time the importance of groups of structures with historic or architectural value. Insall and his team “crawled in overalls” over some 400 buildings, evaluating their merits and advocating that the best ones should be retained.

This led to his appointment as conservation consultant for Chester, and, ultimately, to the establishment of municipal conservation officers in local councils across the country. It also helped formulate many of the principles that underpin today’s conservation management plans and historic building appraisals.

Over time, Insall became a driving force in the workings of the Ancient Monuments Board and the Historic Buildings Council for England. There he befriended the architectural historian John Summerson, and the historians and conservation activists Nikolaus Pevsner and John Betjeman. These liaisons seeded the formation of English Heritage in 1984, of which Insall was a founding commissioner.

Conservation techniques are continually evolving and Insall kept abreast of developments. In the decade-long restoration of Westminster Hall completed in 2020, for instance, nanolime (nano-sized particles of calcium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol) was used to consolidate weathered limestone, and latex poultices employed to remove staining. Insall was also a thoughtful writer, summarising his philosophy, principles and practice in Living Buildings (2008), reprinted a decade later with a foreword by the then Prince of Wales.

For the last three years, Insall projects have won the Europa Nostra award, Europe’s highest accolade for heritage conservation: for the restoration of Westminster Hall (2024), the saving from dereliction of the 18th-century Camellia House at Wentworth Woodhouse, in South Yorkshire (2025) and the revitalisation of Rochdale’s imposing neo-Gothic Town Hall (2026).

Whether resplendent in elegant tweed suits on Instagram, commuting to the office on a BMW 750 motorbike, or vertiginously face to face with Nelson at the top of his column, Insall cultivated a suavely swashbuckling persona, laced with charm and humour. Though he retired as practice chairman in 1998, he continued to work as a consultant until his death.

“Buildings are so very much like people,” he observed. “They all have their own characters, their own strengths and weaknesses, their own message, their own background in terms of the influences that have made them. People change throughout their lives – so does a building.”

Insall was knighted in 2010. He is survived by Libby and their three children, Robert, Christopher and Hilary.

article_text:
Jessica Lange says she feels her acting career might be “coming to an end,” and that her current film, Long Day’s Journey Into Night , wouldn’t be a bad way to go out.

In an interview with Rolling Stone posted yesterday, Lange addressed a wide range of topics and a look back at her own career when she was asked what roles she’d like to tackle in the future. (Watch the interview below.)

“I actually feel like I’m coming to an end,” said Lange, fresh off a dual role in Ryan Murphy’s American Horror Story 13. ” “And maybe it’s not a bad way to end, you know, the last film being Long Day’s Journey Into Night and playing Mary Tyrone .”

Related Stories

Jessica Lange To Receive Vision Award At Sun Valley Film Festival

'Long Day's Journey Into Night' Starring Jessica Lange, Ed Harris & Ben Foster Acquired By Quiver

Lange cited the dearth of roles for women and the difficulty in getting projects off the ground as playing factors in her feelings about the future, a subject that figured into her previous Murphy series Feud: Bette and Joan (she played Joan Crawford to Susan Sarandon’s Bette Davis) and also informs a project she’s been hoping to get underway for some time: A Marlene Dietrich biopic.

Watch on Deadline

“We touched on this with Ryan [Murphy]’s project Feud with Joan and Bette about what happens when an actress gets to a certain age and they’re no longer viable,” Lange said. “That was the theme with Bette and Joan, [and] that is a recurrent theme for a lot of women, especially of that period.” She added that the Dietrich project would focus on “what she did, where she moved on from when Hollywood was kind of finished with her.”

Lange said the Dietrich project is one of a couple that have “been in the works for ever and may or may not happen. It doesn’t seem easy to get things made anymore, at least not the kind of films that interest me.”

Long Day’s Journey Into Night , directed by Jonathan Kent and starring Lange, Ed Harris, Ben Foster and Colin Morgan, was filmed in 2022, six years after Kent and Lange did the Eugene O’Neill play on Broadway (Lange won a Tony Award for her performance). The film was released in the U.S. last month.

Moments after it emerged that Netflix had gotten rid of Bela Bajaria , it named Peter Rice as her replacement.

Former Disney exec Rice takes the job starting October 26.

Rice will oversee all content at Netflix including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.

Related Stories

Netflix Layoffs: Unscripted Casting & Development Execs Impacted

Rice’s last full-time job was as Chairman of Walt Disney Television and Chairman of General Entertainment for The Walt Disney Company. He was fired in June 2022 and replaced by Dana Walden.

He was named Head of Ceremonies and Content for the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games in July 2025.

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: List Of Hollywood & Media Layoffs From Paramount To Warner Bros Discovery To CNN & More

“Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across TV and film is deep and broad,” said Ted Sarandos, Co-CEO, Netflix. “He understands what makes stories resonate, and he’s spent his career helping talent do the best work of their lives. I’m excited to welcome him to Netflix as Chief Content Officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love.”

Rice, whose name started circulating for the Netflix job last week, is a rare executive with high-level experience in both features and TV having run Fox Searchlight and subsequently the Fox Networks Group and Disney’s television operation. One area he does not have a lot of experience — streaming.

“Netflix has fundamentally changed the way stories are made, shared and experienced around the world,” said Rice. “They’ve shown again and again that they’re willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I’m excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere.”

Since leaving Disney, Rice has been producing movies, most recently The Social Reckoning, which opened last weekend.

Internal Email from Ted Sarandos

Hi everyone, I have an important update to share about our Content leadership. After a phenomenal decade at Netflix, Bela is leaving the company. It’s hard to overstate the impact Bela has had during her time here. From expanding our content offering to include the large-scale expansion of unscripted programming and the launches of live events and sports to helping shape the broadening of our content offering around the world. So much of what you see on Netflix today can be traced back to a Bela initiative: Insatiable, Queer Eye, Lupin, You, The Diplomat, WWE, YuYu Hakusho, The Night Agent, Heeramandi: The Diamond Bazaar, Squid Game, Tyson vs Paul, Cien años de soledad, the NFL. She also helped reshape our strategy to focus on fewer, bigger, better movies, championing films like KPop Demon Hunters, The Adventures of Cliff Booth, and Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, as well as bringing award winning films like La Bola Negra and Possible Love to Netflix. A tremendous and diverse range of content (and that’s just a snapshot), bringing joy to our members across so many genres. Bela has built and shaped a truly global Content organization, hiring brilliant people and empowering them to make good decisions. I am incredibly grateful to her for everything she’s done. I know this is a big change in a year that has already had its share. But I also see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in UCAN where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world. To help us seize on this moment, I’m excited to share that we’ve hired a new leader. Peter Rice is joining Netflix as our new Chief Content Officer beginning next week. Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across both TV and film is deep and broad. On the film side, running Fox Searchlight, he helped bring beloved fan favorite films like Slumdog Millionaire, Little Miss Sunshine, Sideways and Juno to screens. And more recently, as Chairman of Walt Disney Television, he led one of the most successful television divisions in the world, where he was responsible for a massive breadth and scale of shows ranging from The Simpsons, American Idol ,and Modern Family, to The Bear, and Abbott Elementary, along with ABC News programming and major sporting events such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup Finals. He’s one of the few people in our industry who has ever operated at the quality and scale that we do at Netflix every day. In the last few years, he has turned his attention to creating and has produced films with Alex Garland, Danny Boyle, Chris Rock, Jason Reitman and Aaron Sorkin at Sony and A24. I’ve gotten to know Peter personally over the years, and I’ve always been impressed by his straightforward approach, the depth of his relationships and his exceptional creative and business instincts. Talent should have the best experiences of their life here, and Peter and I both believe that Netflix can and should be the home of the best storytellers in the world. It’s been an eventful series of days here, and I realize we’ve asked you to absorb a lot of news and a lot of information. But we all know change is what we do at Netflix. Greg and I will host a companywide town hall on Wednesday, October 21. I want everyone to hear how we’re thinking about the strategy and our execution amid this week’s changes, and to have a chance to ask questions. It will be informal and mostly Q&A, so please bring your questions about this week’s changes and anything else on your mind. Please join me in thanking Bela, and welcoming Peter to the team. Ted

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: The Chris Rock directed dramedy, Misty Green , from A24 will hit Netflix on Nov. 9.

While A24’s pay-one output deal with HBO Max, Rock’s first directorial in 12 years lands at Netflix given his long-running relationship with the streamer on its comedy specials.

Misty Green , which made its world premiere at TIFF, is currently playing in limited theaters nationwide.

Rock wrote, directed, and produced the film, and stars alongside Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick, and Topher Grace. The pic follows Eleazar as Misty, a once-promising actress who is fighting for a second act.

The actress’ work has earned a Toronto International Film Festival Tribute Award, the Hamptons Film Festival Breakthrough Performer Award, the Mill Valley Film Festival Spotlight Award, and the Middleburg Film Festival Breakthrough Actor Award. She was also named one of Newport Film Festival x Variety’s “10 Actors to Watch” and will receive a Breakthrough Award at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival later this month.

Watch on Deadline

Deadline Chief Film Critic Pete Hammond praised Eleazar in Misty Green , writing that the movie is “all lifted way up high by Eleazar, who makes this all worth the ticket. She’s mesmerizing in one of the best performances by an actress this year. You believe her; you may even know her.”

Misty Green is produced by incoming Netflix Content Boss Peter Rice, Rock, David Worthen Brooks, Victoria Thomas.

article_text:
Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky , chronicling the making of the 1976 classic Rocky , is set to open the Cairo International Film Festival’s 47th edition in November.

In a timely connection, the choice of film ties in with the fact that Cairo, which is Egypt ‘s oldest film festival, also is marking the 50th anniversary of its creation in 1976, even if it is only at its 47th edition.

Related Stories

‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Peter Farrelly’s Sensational Biopic Of The Making Of Stallone’s Classic Is Just As Inspiring As The Original Movie – Toronto Film Festival

‘I Play Rocky’s Peter Farrelly Talks Why The Making Of ‘Rocky’ Was The Next Real-Life Story He Wanted To Take A Swing At – Toronto Studio

The biopic stars Anthony Ippolito in the role of a young Sylvester Stallone as he struggles to establish himself in Hollywood and bring his passion project Rocky to the big screen, while retaining his place in the lead role.

I Play Rocky world premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September, where it was first runner-up for the People’s Choice Award .

Watch on Deadline

It went on to win the Audience Award in the Galas & Special Presentations section at the Vancouver Film Festival and the Audience Choice Award for Best Feature Film at Canada’s Cinéfest Sudbury Film Festival.

The film also was selected for a surprise screening at the BFI London Film Festival and featured at the Rome, Zurich, and Chicago film festivals, as well as AFI FEST, where it screened in the Red Carpet Premieres section.

RELATED: ‘I Play Rocky’ Trailer: “Do You Believe In Me…Or Not?”; The Ultimate Underdog Story Looks A Knockout

“By selecting I Play Rocky as its opening film, CIFF continues its commitment to showcasing cinema that combines artistic merit with audience appeal, while turning the spotlight on the filmmaking process itself and the personal and creative challenges behind bringing stories to the screen,” the festival said in a release.

“Half a century after Rocky first reached audiences and the Cairo International Film Festival was founded, the opening night of CIFF’s 47th edition brings these two histories together: one celebrating the determination of a young actor who fought to bring his character to life, the other marking a cinematic journey that began in Cairo in 1976 and continues to connect audiences with films from around the world.”

The 47th edition will run November 11-20.
